docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: This datasheet provides an account of the design process and purpose of the elements of the HeatSmith device designed by Malik Johnson.

docs.title: Project Summary
docs.text: The HeatSmith device is a product designed to provide users with an up-to-date accurate reading of the temperature and humidity.

docs.title: My Contribution
docs.text:
This portion of the HeatSmith device is the data processing/UX portion. The design goal here is to balance usability with information delivery and do so at a reasonable cost in both dollars and power. More detail on the rest of the HeatSmith device and the relation between the part described in this datasheet to the wider device found in the team report. To review the details listed of the material used to construct the subsection, you can review it in the "BOM" section of the datasheet.

docs.title: Component Selection
docs.text:
Temperature Display

Solution Pros Cons * Option 1. * MDOB064048AV-WI Midas OLED Screen $8.08/eachlink to product * Inexpensive* Uses a simple 2-Pin I2C Interface * High Contrast * Low Resolution Screen* Undersized. * Option 2. * NHD-C160100DIZ-FSW-FBW Newhaven LCD Screen * $23.53/each * link to product * Color Display * More expensive * Complex Interface * Low Contrast * Option 3. * AES152296A00-2.66ENRS Orient E-Paper Screen * $10.22/each * link to product * Low Power * Perfect Size * Complex Interface

Choice: Option 1: MDOB064048AV-WI Midas OLED Screen

Rationale: The choice is really between the first and last options; the LCD screen is simply overkill for the project's needs. And between those two options, while the E-paper display has its appeal especially with its on-component ram, perfect size for the envisioned project, and low power consumption, the OLED screen's simpler control setup and high-contrast screen make for a better tradeoff, especially as its max power draw is lower than the E-paper's (20 mA vs 25 mA, though the E-paper's power draw is intermittent, hence the lower overall consumption).

Power

Solution Pros Cons * Option 1. * LM7912CT/NOPB Texas Instruments * $1.61/each * link to product * Low Quiescent Current * More expensive * Inverting Output * Option 2. * LM78L12ACZ/NOPB Texas Instruments $0.6/each link to product * Inexpensive * Small *. High Dropout Voltage * Option 2. * L7812CV SMTMicroelectronics * $1.21/each * link to product * High Current Capabilities * More expensive * High Quiescent Current

Choice: Option 1: L7812CV SMTMicroelectronics

Rationale: The second option is out of the running since it lacks the output current to support the screen, leaving it between the first and last options. However, since the first option is slightly more expensive than the third and the difference in performance between the two is pretty negligible (Quiescent current is essentially a non-factor for our purposes), the third is the best choice.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The schematic shown below (available as a pdf here and archived here) is designed to support the user-interaction features of the HeatSmith device, featuring the digital user interface and the heat alarm speaker. The buttons are attached to pull-up resistors to support software on the Curiosity Nano device, while the speaker and OLED screen are controlled via a transistor and an IC2 connection by that same device. The buttons are also usable as debugging features, alongside the debug LED and the internal Curiosity Nano LED (tied to RF3). The design's power comes from two linear voltage regulators attached to a coaxial power connection (presumably connected through a DC adapted to an outlet) and the design connects to the sensors by means of an 8-pin ribbon connection (though only the analog pins, 6 and 7, in use).

Figure above: Showing the schematic in question.

docs.title: Conclusions
docs.text: Given the relatively small consumption of both the microcontroller and the OLED screen (0.52 A in total), the consumption of my portion of the HeatSmith device should fit comfortably within our overall power budget.
